Hi all — I'm Chris Brink, maintainer of thefalsework/papers (https://github.com/thefalsework/papers), an open-source research programme on structural incompleteness across domains (CC-BY-4.0, 6 papers). I'm not a Lean user myself — I'm looking for a collaborator rather than reviewing submissions — but the formalization targets are specified precisely enough that they stand on their own as elementary mathematics.

The primary target is the music-kernel endofunctor formalization from Paper 3 § 4 (v9.1). Six claims, in three tiers:

Tier 1 (elementary; ~20–100 lines each, mathlib has everything needed):

  • Irrationality of log₂(3/2) via FTA. The same FTA argument gives the qualitative non-vanishing of |12·Real.log 3 − 19·Real.log 2| (the Pythagorean comma as a linear-form-in-logs statement) — logically the same claim restated.
  • Fix(D) = {∅} for D(X) = X ∪ (X + α) on finite subsets of UnitAddCircle (= AddCircle (1 : ℝ) ≃ ℝ/ℤ), by cardinality.

Tier 2 (intermediate; mathlib has the frameworks, glue required):

  • Lambek's lemma applied to this C and D ⇒ no terminal coalgebra for D.
  • Weyl equidistribution (or just density) ⇒ colimit of D-iteration escapes the ambient category.

Tier 3 (advanced / requires additional mathlib development):

  • ℤ/12ℤ quotient structure and the H = ⟨4⟩ (Giant Steps) substructure.
  • Effective quantitative bound from Baker's 1966 theorem on linear forms in logarithms. Baker's theorem is not currently in mathlib — this is a long-horizon target rather than a first PR; the qualitative case is already covered in Tier 1.

Specs with paper cross-references:

  • Claim statements: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/tree/main/validation/claims
  • Formalization target README: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/lean/README.md

A first contribution picking either Tier 1 point would be very welcome. Happy to discuss approaches, review early drafts, and credit contributors by name in the paper's revision note. The repo's CONTRIBUTING.md has acceptance criteria for formalization PRs.

The broader theoretical framing isn't a prerequisite — the six points are elementary math. Questions about the framing are welcome; the repo is the best place for them.

— Chris (chris@falsework.dev)

I want to comment on https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/papers/pythagorean-shared-floor/pythagorean.md#2-the-pythagorean-comma-statement-and-context.

First of all, a great video on the topic: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q9maEvJP8Nk

You write

The next convergent, 31/53

But the next convergent in your series is 24/41.

It is a mathematical fact about how log₂(3/2) sits in the reals, and it determines the set of temperaments that are practically useful for closing the fifth-octave cycle.

Only if your goal is to optimize the accuracy of perfect fifth. But there's more to music than perfect fifths, and some tuning sacrifice accuracy of perfect fifth to improve approximations of other harmonics.

A good example is 31 tone equal temperament: it has slightly worse fifths than 12 tone equal temperament (5 cents off instead of 2), but is an effective 11-limit temperament with excellent 5th (major thirds) and 7th (harmonic sevenths) harmonics.

even though 53-TET is impractical for keyboard construction

It's not completely impractical: for example, Lumatone exists. But 31 tet and 41 tet are more popular. There's also a guitar for playing in 41 tet called Kite guitar.

Thank you — these are all right, all three.

  1. Convergents. The paper's § 2.2 lists the continued-fraction convergents of log₂(3/2) as 0/1, 1/1, 1/2, 3/5, 7/12, 24/41, 31/53, ... — correctly — and then in the very next sentence refers to "the next convergent, 31/53," skipping 24/41 entirely. Straightforward factual error. Will correct to the full sequence in the prose.

  2. Scope of "practically usable temperaments." You're right that this is narrower than the paper currently claims. What Baker + the continued-fraction structure of log₂(3/2) picks out is the set of EDOs optimal for approximating log₂(3/2) specifically — the rank-2, 3-limit problem. 31-TET is the classical 5/7/11-limit target (Huygens 1691, Fokker); 41-TET is a good 7-limit temperament (hence the Kite guitar, which I didn't know about — thanks); 53-TET is the specifically-3-limit continued-fraction hit (Mercator, Bosanquet). Each is optimal for a different linear-form-in-logs problem, and the paper currently reads as if 12-TET and 53-TET were uniquely practically usable, which isn't right. Will rescope §§ 2.2, 4.2, and 7.1 explicitly to "optimizing the approximation to log₂(3/2)" rather than to unqualified "practically usable," and will point forward to § 6.1 (Refusal, where the broader microtonal practice already lives in the paper).

  3. "53-TET is impractical for keyboard construction." Dated. Lumatone is a real instrument, the Kite guitar is real, and the microtonal performance tradition has real infrastructure. Will rewrite — probably something like "53-TET has historically required specialized instruments; contemporary implementations include the Lumatone keyboard."

Thanks for the video — will watch.

These will go into v1.2 of the paper. Filing a tracking issue right now so the corrections are in the validation queue before they're applied. If you want to keep poking at other sections of this or any of the other papers, GitHub issues on https://github.com/thefalsework/papers are the best persistent home — I'll receive comments here on Zulip too, but GitHub is where this stays visible to future readers.

Also: if you're comfortable being credited by name in the v1.2 revision note, let me know what attribution you'd like (Zulip display name, full name, GitHub handle, or anonymous). Happy with any of those.

Genuinely grateful — this is the validation architecture doing its job.
Are you using AI to write these messages? This is strongly discouraged here.
It is even disallowed now. Please use your own words.

Note the core topic here about the math of tuning systems is a legitimate topic that I personally find very interesting, but unfortunately this seems to be interspersed with heavy usage of AI in a way that doesn't make sense.

If anyone is unfamiliar but interested in this area, I suggest the series of blog posts by John Baez now being assembled into a book: https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/tuning_book/

I've thought before about what any of this would look like in Lean. The most interesting part is likely thinking about and setting up the exact statement of what you want to verify! For instance, you could probably do something about the relationship between "optimal" N-TET and the corresponding continued fraction.

Kevin, Michael: fair and understood. I was drafting with AI help. I won't do that for posts here from now on.

Chris Henson: thanks, the Baez work is new to me, I'll look at it. And thanks for distinguishing the topic from the AI concern.

Your point about "setting up the exact statement" is where most of the work on this side sits, I think. Paper 5 § 2.2 tries to pull out the relationship between optimal N-TET and the continued fraction of log₂(3/2). The convergents 7/12, 24/41, 31/53 are the equal temperaments that minimize the Pythagorean comma, and the paper says so, but it doesn't state the theorem that picks them out as such. That's the piece I can't do on my own. If you ever wanted to read https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/validation/claims/music-kernel-01-irrationality.md or https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/validation/claims/music-kernel-06-baker.md and say the statement is wrong or too loose, that's more useful than a proof at this stage. The question right now is whether the statements are even set up right to be provable.

Plainly stated: This is my solo research. No lab, no team, no funding, no institutional affiliation. The papers make claims that need specialist review and I can't review my own from the inside, which is why the repo is set up the way it is. Every claim flagged for validation has a claim file, an issue, and a place to move to once it is corrected or confirmed. suhr's corrections above now sit in Paper 5 v1.2, in https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/validation/RESOLVED.md, and in https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md. Dmitri Tymoczko (Princeton, A Geometry of Music) and James Cutting (Cornell, cinema perception) corresponded with me on the music-kernel Coltrane classification and the cinema-kernel criteria respectively. Both are documented at the same RESOLVED.md under Corroboration with explicit scope limits.

Paper 2 of the series is specifically about this question. The argument, in short, is that AI-assisted scholarship can't function honestly without a disclosed correction architecture, and the rest of the repo is structured around that argument. I won't make the case here on Zulip, but the AI disclosure is in the README and the correction record is in the validation directory.

GitHub issues on thefalsework/papers email chris@falsework.dev

Chris

Chris Henson said:

If anyone is unfamiliar but interested in this area, I suggest the series of blog posts by John Baez now being assembled into a book: https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/tuning_book/

I would also recommend Xen Wiki.

By the way, the theory of MOS scales generalizes finding temperaments with continued fractions. For example, if your generator is perfect fifth, you can start from https://en.xen.wiki/w/5L_2s and then take its daughters until you find an equal temperament with desired perfect fifth size. This corresponds to walking Stern-Brocot tree as illustrated at https://en.xen.wiki/w/Scale_tree.
Another approach for finding equal temperaments is described at https://en.xen.wiki/w/The_Riemann_zeta_function_and_tuning. It optimizes for all harmonics.
Even here I can't escape the microtonalists... haha
